The "Weekend of Blood" —
Situating the January 2026 Iran Massacre within the Global History of State Violence

The events of January 8–9, 2026, in the Islamic Republic of Iran represent a catastrophic inflection point in the global history of state violence. In this document, we argue that the verified floor of the death toll of Iranian protesters during the January 2026 crackdown in Iran is not only unprecedented in Iran, but also represents a statistically unique and extreme anomaly in the history of state violence against civilian protest movements worldwide.

Data: Establishing The Verified Floor
The high-end estimates of the 2026 Iran massacre, as reported by several reputable international media outlets surpass 30,000 deaths [1, 2]. However, to analyze the scale of this violence, we look at the most conservative, verified data rather than the fluctuating high-end estimates. As of February 1st, 2026, the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) has confirmed the identities of a total of 6,842 victims within the first thirty-six days of the protests, with the vast majority occurring during the January 8–9 window [3]. Among those, HRANA reports recording 6,425 individuals as “protesters”, including 146 minors; 214 as members of government‑affiliated forces and 57 as “civilian non‑protesters” [3]. An additional 11,280 deaths remain under review by HRANA at the time of writing this report [3]. In this report, we will use the 6,842 figure as it represents the "verified floor"—individuals whose identities and deaths have been meticulously documented despite the intentional disruption of the internet in Iran.

Simultaneously, the Iranian government’s officially admitted toll—typically used as a tool of downplaying atrocities—stands at 3,117 deaths. This figure is substantially lower than independent tallies, reflecting consistent under‑reporting in official statistics [4].

What Makes This A “Crime Against Humanity”?
The classification of the January 2026 crackdown as Crimes Against Humanity is supported by a burgeoning international legal consensus. According to the Rome Statute [5], such crimes consist of acts—including murder, imprisonment, and torture—committed as part of a 'widespread or systematic attack directed against any civilian population.' The Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI) and Amnesty International have documented that the 2026 massacre was not a series of scattered escalations, but a "coordinated nationwide escalation" in the use of lethal force [6, 7]. This is evidenced by the "organized" state response across "all 31 of Iran’s provinces," involving the simultaneous deployment of military-grade weaponry—including "DShK machine guns" and "snipers" positioned on rooftops [6, 8]. Furthermore, the state implemented what observers describe as a systematic targeting of medical neutrality, where security forces "removed wounded protesters from hospitals," "fired into the faces of victims at close range," and carried out the "arrests and prosecutions of doctors" treating the injured [6, 8]. The CHRI asserts that the "intensity and rate of the mass killings," characterized by the deliberate "targeting of protesters' heads and torsos," meets the threshold for international atrocity crimes [6, 7]. This legal standing was solidified by the UN Human Rights Council's emergency resolution on January 23, which extended the Fact-Finding Mission’s mandate specifically to investigate these crimes under international law [8].

Comparative Historical Analysis
The lethal intensity of the 2026 crackdown is unprecedented in the Islamic Republic’s history of violently suppressing dissent since 1979 [6]. The 2026 massacre follows the precedent of 'Bloody November' in 2019 in Iran, where a total telecommunication blackout facilitated a five-day crackdown that resulted in the deaths of approximately 1,500 protesters according to Interior Ministry officials—a figure that, while significantly lower than current investigative estimates, was the bloodiest suppression in the country since the 1979 Revolution [9].

The 2026 massacre is a calculated repetition of the "Bloody November" strategy of 2019. In both instances, the violence was inextricably linked to a total national internet and telecommunications blackout, to facilitate mass killing away from international scrutiny.  By severing the logic layer of the network and jamming satellite signals, the regime decoupled the act of killing from the global community's ability to witness it in real-time [10]. This repeated use of “Digital Blackout” to facilitate mass killing is an instrument of impunity by design [11]. Under international legal standards, such a coordinated effort should be interpreted as a hallmark of systematic intent to commit atrocity crimes.

To situate the January 8–9 events within global history of state violence against civilian protest movements, we use data collected by the Nonviolent and Violent Campaigns and Outcomes (NAVCO) project. Historical data suggests that between 1946 and 2013, the average unarmed revolution suffered approximately 105 deaths per year [12]. While regimes respond with lethal force in nearly 88% of nonviolent uprisings, "mass killings"—defined as episodes where at least 1,000 unarmed civilians are killed—occur in only about 23% of cases [12].

The international community has historically used the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre as the primary reference point for state-led suppression of domestic protest. In the historical massacre at Tiananmen Square (1989), the death toll was estimated to be "hundreds to thousands" [12]. An official report issued by the Chinese authorities claimed that “more than 3,000 civilians were wounded and over 200, including 36 college students, died during the riot”, according to Amnesty International [13]. Whereas the Red Cross Society of China reportedly provided an early estimate of Approx. 2,600 deaths, based on data collected from various hospitals in Beijing [14]. Therefore, the Iran crackdown exceeds the confirmed lethality of the 1989 crackdown in Beijing.

The toll also far exceeds other notorious crackdowns [12]. In Egypt, during the Rabaa Massacre (2013), following the coup against Mohammed Morsi, the Egyptian Army massacred nearly 1,000 Muslim Brotherhood activists who were protesting [12]. In the Amritsar Massacre (1919), British colonial forces in India fired into a crowd of nonviolent protesters, killing hundreds (cited as 200–300 in colonial records) and injuring over 1,000  [12]. During the Dili Massacre (1991), Indonesian forces killed approximately 250 civilians in East Timor attending a funeral for an independence activist [12]. In the Khartoum Massacre in Sudan (2019) Security forces stormed a protest camp, killing over 100 people and dumping bodies in the Nile River  [12].

While the Syrian Revolution (2011–2026) resulted in over 230,000 deaths, those casualties were the product of a fifteen-year multi-front civil war involving heavy artillery, air raids, and foreign intervention. Even when compared to the bloodiest "crackdown phases" of the Syrian uprising, such as the Daraya or Ghouta massacres, the scale of the Iranian event is distinct. The most lethal single-day atrocity of the Syrian Revolution—the 2013 Ghouta chemical attack, which claimed approximately 1,429 lives according to U.S. intelligence assessments [15]. Unlike the gradual escalation of the Syrian Revolution (2011) or the localized horrors of the Srebrenica massacre (1995), the January 2026 violence in Iran should be characterized by an unprecedented "lethality-to-time" ratio, given that it was a singular, state-led massacre executed against a domestic civilian population within a non-war setting.

Conclusion & Call to Action
At the time of writing this report, the verified floor of casualties (6,842) already reveals a concentration of state lethality in a single weekend that is statistically more intense than any comparable domestic suppression event in modern history. This represents a quantitative and qualitative shift in state violence that the world has yet to fully grasp.

Once the investigative estimates by HRANA are eventually confirmed, the lethality of the 2026 Iran Massacre may exceed the confirmed lethality of events like Tiananmen (1989) by an order of magnitude, standing as the deadliest state-led crackdown on a domestic protest movement in a singular event in at least the last 100 years of global history!
To prevent this "Silence-Kill" protocol from becoming a global blueprint for impunity, the international community must transition from condemnation to an active protection strategy, centered on three urgent pillars:

First, the international community must treat the ongoing internet disruption in Iran as a primary tactical weapon of the massacre. We call for Digital Humanitarian Intervention, including the mass deployment of satellite-based technologies to restore the "witness layer" and neutralize the regime’s military-grade jamming and restore the digital sovereignty of Iranians.

Second, the world must confront the Judicial Blockade surrounding the “expedited” prosecution of nearly 49,070 detainees [16], including many medical staff and lawyers [17]. Unverified claims made by the US president regarding the suspension of executions [18] must not distract from the reality that the Iranian judiciary has explicitly urged punishment "as quickly as possible" and "without leniency," utilizing the capital charge of Moharebeh (“enmity against God”) to facilitate state-sanctioned murder [8].

Finally, because the Iranian state has actively weaponized its sovereignty to commit mass murder, the criteria for the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) have been met. Under the R2P framework, when a state is the manifest perpetrator of crimes against humanity, the international community’s responsibility to intervene becomes mandatory, and protecting the rights of individuals takes precedence over the sovereignty of hostile states ruling over them. This warrants the immediate activation of international justice mechanisms, including the pursuit of universal jurisdiction and a formal referral to the International Criminal Court.

If the international community continues to view these events through the lens of "unrest" rather than a singular, concentrated massacre that is a clear departure from the historical norms of the 21st-century, it risks normalizing unprecedented levels of state violence.

The video, filmed on a beach in northern France, shows young men in life jackets throwing stones at officers to keep them away from their dinghy – forcing them to use Pava spray before slashing the inflatable with a knife.

The footage, captured by gendarmes and shared by the UK's Border Security Command, was presented as evidence the French are taking a 'bold' and aggressive approach to halting small boat crossings after signing a new deal with Britain. 

But shadow home secretary Chris Philp called Labour's celebration of the deal's results 'a joke' and insisted that instances of crossings being prevented were falling.

'The only way we can stop the crossings is by having a proper deterrent,' he said, calling for irregular arrivals to be 'rapidly' deported. 

Officers and gendarmes have repeatedly been seen failing to intervene as boats are launched, including in a recent clip filmed by Mr Philp.

French police stopped more than 4,300 migrants from reaching the UK in the first three months of a new deal between the countries, according to Home Office data. 

A total of 185 boat crossings were blocked between April 27 and August 2, representing around 60 per cent of attempts. Yet many are still getting through, with 8,200 migrants successfully arriving on 120 boats over the same period.

More than 3,000 migrants have arrived since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister, loading pressure on him to come up with a new plan for tackling illegal migration amid a growing backlash at the cost – and impact on local communities – of housing asylum seekers.

The data also suggests French police are mainly stopping smaller vessels, rather than the mega-dinghies that smugglers are increasingly using to ferry as many as 230 migrants at a time. 

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, claimed the interception figures showed that the deal with the French was 'already having a real impact, stopping crossings before they happen and disrupting the criminal gangs behind them'.

text:
✈️ SpiceJet: How a 12% Market Share Airline Became a 1.5% Zombie

Stock down 70% in one year. ₹40 to ₹11. 
Market cap ₹1,640 Cr.

 Negative equity of ₹2,800 Cr. 

20+ insolvency petitions filed.

Still flying.

How is SpiceJet even alive? The answer is fascinating and not in a good way.

📉 The collapse in numbers:

→ Market share: 12.5% (FY21) → 4.0% (FY24) → 1.5% (mid-2026)

→ Revenue: ₹8,869 Cr (FY23) → ₹4,786 Cr (TTM)

→ Shareholder equity: Negative ₹2,800 Cr

→ Working capital deficit: ₹4,277 Cr

→ Accumulated losses: ₹8,638 Cr

→ Promoter pledging: 39.77%

A 46% revenue collapse in 3 years. While Indian aviation grew 10%+ annually.

This is not a market problem.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

❌ What went wrong?

Classic death spiral.

SpiceJet couldn't pay lessors. Lessors grounded planes.

Fewer planes meant less revenue. Less revenue meant more defaults. More defaults meant more groundings.

Fleet got cannibalized for spare parts. Maintenance deferred. On-Time Performance collapsed to 26-34%. (IndiGo runs 80%+.)

Corporate contracts vanished. High-yield passengers left.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚖️ Why no bankruptcy?

20+ NCLT petitions since 2023. Not one admitted.

The playbook:

Contest petition → Delay → Wait until NCLT reserves order → Settle out-of-court at the last minute → Creditor withdraws.

August 2026: SpiceJet settled with Aviator ML the day NCLT was pronouncing orders on 8 cases.

Paid $500K.

All cases deferred.

NCLT fined both parties ₹15 lakh for wasting judicial time.

Why do lessors accept?

SpiceJet owns nothing. Planes are leased. Engines are leased.

Liquidation yields 10 cents. Settlement yields 40 cents.

Lessors take the haircut.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💰 How does it keep flying?

→ QIP (Sept 2024): Raised ₹3,000 Cr at ₹61.60/share. Stock now ₹11.

Investors down 82%.

→ Debt-to-equity swaps: Carlyle converted lease dues into 10.4 Cr shares.

→ Continuous dilution: Equity base expanded 19% in one year.

Every capital raise dilutes shareholders.

Stock falls.

Next raise is more dilutive.

Treadmill.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

📊 The market moved on.

→ IndiGo: 67.4% share

→ Air India Group: 24.0%

→ Everyone else: 8.6%

Two players control 91% of domestic aviation.

SpiceJet is fighting for scraps against Akasa and regional carriers.

Prime slots at Mumbai, Delhi, Bangalore?

Gone.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🎯 The bottom line.

SpiceJet is not investable. It's a case study.

When a company's primary skill becomes avoiding bankruptcy rather than generating profits, the equity is not an investment it's a speculation on survival.

At negative book value, any stake is a call option on perfect execution in a market where competitors control 91% of traffic.

Ajay Singh is skilled at survival.

But survival ≠ shareholder value.

Not advice. Just observations.

text:
A Finnish parliamentarian has been blocked  from entering the UK to give an address on freedom of speech at a  conference this week, following her criminal conviction for “hate  speech” by Finland’s Supreme Court.

Longstanding Christian politician Päivi  Räsänen, who is a member of the Finnish Parliament’s “Friends of the  United Kingdom” group, was due to give a talk in person this week about  freedom of speech, at a religious freedom conference.

However, in July, Räsänen was informed  that her Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) to the UK had been  cancelled, despite her application initially being approved in June.

Räsänen will be forced to speak at the  event virtually on Wednesday and Friday, unless she is granted entry to  the country. The Finnish MP and ADF are now calling on the UK Home  Secretary Shabana Mahmood to make a last-minute intervention, to allow  Räsänen to attend in person on Friday.

This follows the Finnish grandmother and former Interior Minister’s “hate speech” conviction by  the Finnish Supreme Court in March 2026, for expressing her Christian  beliefs on marriage and human sexuality in a 2004 booklet written for  her church.

Räsänen’s criminal conviction was noted with concern by observers around the world, including the US State Department and the US Religious Liberty Commission, which was established by President Donald Trump.

Lutheran Bishop Juhana Pohjola, who was  criminally convicted alongside Räsänen for publishing her booklet, was  also blocked from entering the UK, after his ETA was denied in June.

After her ETA was cancelled, Räsänen  subsequently applied for a full visa and wrote to the UK Home Secretary  personally to ask that it be granted ahead of the conference this week.

To date, Räsänen has not received an  answer from the Home Secretary, and was informed that she would not be  given a response on her visa application in time to travel for the  event.

Räsänen, Bishop Pohjola and the Luther Foundation Finland, who were all convicted in March over Räsänen’s booklet, have appealed their  cases to the European Court of Human Rights, where they will be  represented by free speech legal advocacy organisation Alliance  Defending Freedom.

Räsänen said: “It is shocking that the  UK has blocked me, a democratically elected politician in an allied  European state, from entering the country.

“I was convicted of ‘hate speech’ in  Finland for peacefully expressing my Christian views. This was an  egregious case of state censorship, noted with concern by observers  around the world, including the US State Department and the US Religious  Liberty Commission.

“Even though this unjust conviction is  currently on appeal to the European Court of Human Rights, the UK has  likely refused me travel authorisation on this basis. In doing so, the  UK is punishing me for exercising my fundamental human rights.

“I call on Home Secretary Shabana  Mahmood to urgently intervene to allow me to enter the UK to speak at  this event. There is still time for this censorship to be reversed.”

Lorcán Price, legal counsel for Alliance  Defending Freedom, representing Räsänen, Bishop Pohjola and the Luther  Foundation Finland at the European Court of Human Rights, said: “In essence Päivi Räsänen has been blocked from entering the UK for peacefully expressing her Christian beliefs.

“This is not an isolated incident. The  UK has in the last year blocked a number of mainstream conservative  individuals, politicians, and now even a member of the Finnish  Parliament and a Lutheran bishop, from entering the country. This trend  is yet another example of the severe and escalating censorship crisis in  Great Britain.

“Furthermore, the British state is  increasingly cracking down on the rights of Christians in the UK:  Christians have been criminalised for silently praying, offering to  speak with people, publicly preaching their faith, and now they have  been blocked from entering the country for expressing their views.

“Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood should  act immediately to allow my client to enter the country, to speak in  person at the religious liberty event in Northern Ireland. Any further  silence on the Home Secretary’s part will reinforce to the British  people and observers around the world that this government has a  deep-seated antipathy to free speech.”

Bishop Pohjola said: “It is an Orwellian reality that I was blocked from entering the UK by the British state.

“For a senior Lutheran cleric to be  criminally sanctioned in one European country and blocked from entering  another, for merely publishing a church booklet which peacefully  expressed views the Finnish state disagreed with, is extremely alarming.

“It shows how far our civilisation has  strayed not only from its Christian roots, but even from respecting the  basic human rights of free speech and religious freedom. The two are  undoubtedly related, as a new secular orthodoxy has taken root across  Western countries, under which dissenters are punished harshly.

“I sincerely hope the UK Home  Secretary acts to allow Paivi to enter the country, and that the  European Court of Human Rights upholds our right to free speech.  Peacefully expressing views on marriage and human sexuality that  Christians have always held is not a crime.”

Background

The former Finnish Interior Minister,  medical doctor and grandmother of 12 was criminally prosecuted for  nearly seven years for sharing her Christian beliefs about marriage and  human sexuality in a 2019 tweet and live radio debate, as well as for  authoring a 2004 church booklet, for which she was charged alongside  Bishop Pohjola and the Luther Foundation Finland.

In 2021, Räsänen was formally charged with  “agitation against a minority group” under a section of the Finnish  criminal code titled “war crimes and crimes against humanity”.

Following unanimous acquittals on all  charges by two lower courts in 2022 and 2023, the state prosecutor  appealed again to the Finnish Supreme Court, regarding the tweet and  church booklet.

The case was heard in October 2025, and in  March 2026, in a narrow 3–2 decision, the Supreme Court upheld the  acquittal for the Bible verse tweet, but convicted Räsänen,  Bishop Pohjola and the Luther Foundation Finland for the 2004 booklet.  The radio show charge was not appealed to the Supreme Court, so that  acquittal stands.

The Supreme Court convicted Räsänen under  a law that was introduced years after the booklet was published, and  did so despite the court’s admission that the booklet “did not contain  incitement to violence or comparable threat-like fomenting of hatred”.

Christian Finnish Parliamentarian Blocked From Entering UK To Discuss Free Speech At Religious Liberty Conference

In an alarming display of censorship, the  Supreme Court fined Räsänen, Bishop Pohjola, and the Luther Foundation  Finland several thousand euros each, and ruled that the condemned  statements within the booklet must be “removed from public access and  destroyed”.

The US State Department commented on  Räsänen’s criminal prosecution, prior to her conviction in March: “In a  democracy, no one should face trial for peacefully sharing their  beliefs. The case against Finnish MP Päivi Räsänen, which accuses her of  hate speech for simply posting a Bible verse, is baseless, as two  courts have unanimously found.”

Following her conviction, the U.S. Embassy Finland said:  “A troubling ruling for religious freedom and freedom of expression:  Finland’s Supreme Court dismissed the charge over MP Päivi Räsänen’s  2019 Bible-verse social-media post, but convicted her over separate  passages in a Christian pamphlet and imposed a fine. Whatever one thinks  of the underlying views, the imposition of criminal liability for  nonviolent religious expression sets a troubling precedent for religious  freedom and freedom of expression.”

The U.S. Supreme Court handed the Trump administration a huge win Monday by allowing an executive order designed to sharply curtail mail voting to go into effect — a move that California and other Democratic-led states have warned could thrust the midterm elections into chaos.

Rushing through unprecedented changes to the mail voting system will be especially challenging for California, where more than 80% of voters use mail ballots and every registered voter receives a ballot by mail. 

In an unsigned ruling, apparently by a 6-3 vote, the court said the states could not show they would be harmed by the restrictions on mail voting and therefore lacked legal standing to challenge it in court.

President Donald Trump’s executive order merely requires his Department of Homeland Security to “prioritize” the investigation and prosecution of those who violate the new voting rules, the court majority said. “It imposes no obligations on the States, so they suffer no concrete harm,” the justices concluded.

In dissent, Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan said the Trump administration has made it clear that it would use its newly granted authority to investigate and prosecute any alleged violators, including representatives of the states. And Justice Kentanji Brown Jackson, the court’s third Democratic appointee, said the court’s order “injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.”

Trump has sought for years to cast doubt on the validity of U.S. elections, often by touting outright lies or making claims that are not backed by any evidence. Mail voting in particular has been a fixation for Trump: He has called the process “cheating” and said in a primetime address in July that “mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt.” He has not, however, raised any concerns about the two elections in which he won the presidency. 

Trump signed an executive order in March that would require states to submit lists of eligible voters to the U.S. Postal Service. Anyone not on the list would be barred from receiving a ballot by mail. The order would also require states to track each mail ballot using a barcode, and would “prioritize” federal prosecution of election officials who send ballots to anyone who’s ineligible to vote.

A federal judge had blocked Trump’s order from going into effect before the midterms, but did not weigh in on the legality of the provisions. An appellate court declined to reverse the injunction, and the Trump administration filed an emergency order asking the Supreme Court to lift it late last month.

California dubbed the order a “ballot-interception program” and argued that it would create insurmountable hurdles for election officials, while disenfranchising voters who would inevitably be confused by the new rules.

Implementing the order before November will now require state and local election officials to divert time and money they normally spend prepping for an election to instead prepare and update the new postal service list, train election officials on a new program, and reformat and reorder ballot envelopes. 

The Postal Service published a rule Friday that calls on states to provide the agency a list of voters who received mail-in ballots. The new rule aligns the Postal Service with Trump’s March 31 executive order.

“Any state that intends to receive mail-in or absentee ballots from individual voters through the Postal Service must ensure that such individuals have been enrolled with the Postal Service for inclusion on the state’s Mail-In and Absentee Participation List,” the new rule says.

“We’re going to be very focused on what we need to do to communicate with voters and fully comply with the law,” Contra Costa County Clerk-Recorder Kristin Connelly told the Chronicle on Monday. “The thing that’s very important to me as registrar is to ensure no one loses access. We are very close to an election. Tomorrow will be 10 weeks out, just 70 days. It’s really critical to focus our time and resources on ways to ensure no one is disenfranchised. I’m very concerned about the confusion this will cause with voters.”

In a brief filed earlier this month, Trump argued that the states’ lawsuit was premature and massively downplayed the executive orders and their potential impact, accusing California of “fearmongering.”

The order “respects States’ role in administering elections and verifying voter eligibility and registration,” D. John Sauer, the U.S. solicitor general, wrote. “It simply directs executive branch agencies to take a modest, commonsense approach to election integrity by providing States and the federal government with tools to combat fraud in federal elections.”

Lower courts will still have to weigh Trump’s order itself, and decide whether its requirements are legal. But for now, the administration appears to have a green light to begin imposing the order.

At the same time, Gov. Gavin Newsom and other California Democrats are advancing legislation that seeks to prevent Trump from interfering in the state’s elections. Last week, at Newsom’s urging, lawmakers introduced a measure that would ban officials from seizing or ordering the seizure of ballots, election records and voting machines before an election is certified. A second bill would ban officials from interfering with a ballot’s delivery to a voter or local election official.

Newsom called for both measures last month in a video posted to social media, in which he said they were aimed at “anyone considering helping President Trump interfere with our election.”

“You will be prosecuted,” Newsom said. “We will be the wall he cannot get past.”

Lawmakers moved to consider the measures in committee, an early step in the legislative process before a bill can become law, on Monday shortly before the Supreme Court announced the decision. Lawmakers have a week to pass the legislation so Newsom can sign it into law.

Once the decision came down, Newsom quickly criticized it.

“Another day, another Trump attempt to rig elections and destroy democracy,” Newsom wrote in a social media post. “We can stop this. VOTE this November.”

Kathryn Palmer and Sophia Bollag contributed to this report.

text:
Goods were received, GST was paid to registered suppliers through banking channels, yet ITC was denied for the suppliers’ default — Gauhati High Court quashed the demand against the bona fide Assessee.

Issue:
Whether ITC could be denied and tax, interest and penalty recovered from the Assessee merely because the selling suppliers allegedly failed to discharge their GST liability, despite receipt of goods, payment of consideration including GST through banking channels and compliance with statutory requirements.

Rule:
A bona fide purchasing dealer who transacts with a registered supplier and fulfils the statutory requirements cannot be denied ITC merely because the supplier fails to deposit the tax collected. The Department’s remedy is to proceed against the defaulting supplier. However, action can be taken against the purchaser where material establishes that the transaction was not bona fide or involved collusion.

Application:
The Assessee had purchased goods during 2017-18 and 2018-19, received the goods, paid the value along with GST through banking channels and produced invoices, GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and other records before the authorities. A search also did not result in recovery of any incriminating material. The ITC demand was nevertheless confirmed principally on the allegation that the suppliers had failed to discharge their tax liability.

Conclusion :
Following National Plasto Moulding v. State of Assam, and the principle in On Quest Merchandising India Pvt. Ltd. v. Government of NCT of Delhi, the Court held that a bona fide Assessee cannot be punished for the supplier’s failure to deposit GST. Accordingly, the Order-in-Original dated 19.02.2024 and Order-in-Appeal dated 14.02.2025 were set aside and quashed. The Department was left free to proceed if material existed showing that the transactions were non-bona fide or collusive.

Impact Analysis:
The judgment protects bona fide purchasers from losing ITC solely due to a supplier’s tax default. The Department must target the defaulting supplier, unless it can establish lack of bona fides or collusion by the purchaser.

🚨 TAX ALERT: Income Tax Department Can Sustain a Look Out Circular (LOC) Where Material Shows Potential Detriment to India’s Economic Interests — Courts Cannot Reassess Sufficiency of Such Material

🔹 What Happened: The Assessee, engaged in garment exports, was subjected to search and seizure proceedings under Section 132(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in February 2019. An LOC was thereafter issued at the instance of the Department on the ground of alleged undisclosed foreign assets/interests and possible liability under the Income-tax Act, Black Money Act, 2015 and PMLA. The Single Judge quashed the LOC, principally holding that its continuance was unsupported by sufficient evidence and infringed the Assessee’s right to travel and livelihood under Article 21.

🔍 Key Takeaways:
• Compliance/Documentation: Under the amended para 8(j) of the 2017 MHA Office Memorandum, an LOC may be issued in exceptional cases where, based on inputs received, the departure of a person appears “detrimental to the … economic interests of India”. The power flows from executive instructions and the subjective satisfaction is primarily that of the authority issuing the LOC.

• Judicial Review: Judicial review of an LOC is not completely barred, but the Court cannot sit in appeal over the authority’s subjective satisfaction or independently assess the qualitative or quantitative sufficiency of the material. Interference is warranted where the material is merely speculative or “moonshine”, or the decision is shockingly disproportionate.

• Economic Interest: In matters concerning fiscal/economic interests, the executive is accorded substantial latitude, as the competent tax authorities are better placed to assess where the economic interests of the country lie. Courts cannot substitute their own subjective view for that of the executive.

• Present Case: The official record contained material concerning alleged large-scale bogus purchases, undisclosed transactions and foreign interests/assets. The Court found that the Department’s decision was not based on irrelevant, inadmissible or insubstantial material. Hence, the LOC could not be quashed merely because the Court might have assessed the material differently.

• Outcome: The Division Bench allowed the Department’s appeal, quashed the Single Judge’s judgment and dismissed the Assessee’s writ petition, with no order as to costs.

⚖️ Legal Reference: Section 132(1), Income-tax Act, 1961 | Para 8(j), MHA Office Memorandum dated 5 December 2017 | Article 21, Constitution of India | Income Tax Department v. Vikas Chaudhary & Ors., decided 12 August 2026.

"How the Supreme Court’s trans ruling is paving the way for a return of gender-neutral loos

The ruling could see a renewed push for unisex lavatories – but critics say the facilities may create safeguarding risks

As businesses and organisations grapple with the implications of last week’s Supreme Court ruling on “sex” meaning “biological sex”, one particular issue appears – once again – to be at the forefront of the gender debate: lavatories.

Which facilities should men who identify as women now use? What about trans men (women who identify as men)? Or even those who identify as non-binary?

Coincidentally, on Wednesday, a judge in Scotland ordered that Scottish schools should provide single-sex toilets, in response to a claim brought against Scottish Borders Council (SBC). The local authority had installed gender-neutral toilets at a primary school, to the chagrin of parents who believed that boys and girls should have access to separate loos.

But campaigners fear that last week’s Supreme Court ruling, which led to the Government saying that trans women should use toilets according to their biological sex, will simply lead to a renewed push for gender-neutral or unisex lavatories, which have also proved highly divisive. Those facilities sometimes involve women sharing with men using urinals, or rows of cubicles used by both sexes.

“What trans person will now use a public lavatory without fear of abuse, or worse?” said Sir Stephen Wall, a former senior civil servant and LGBT activist. “If the Government is serious about human rights, it should mandate the provision of gender-neutral facilities wherever separate provision is at present made for men and women.”

Baroness Falkner of Margravine, who chairs the UK’s Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has said that the ruling brought clarity and that facilities “must be based on biological sex”. But she suggested that many organisations may need to provide a “third space” for trans customers or employees.

Nightclubs in the late 1990s were the first to experiment with gender-neutral toilets Credit: Charday Penn

“There isn’t any law saying you cannot use a neutral third space and they should be using their powers of advocacy to ask for those third spaces.”

Only last year, the Conservative government’s changes to building regulations meant that new restaurants, shopping centres, offices and public toilets would have to feature separate single-sex lavatories for women and men. The new legislation followed government consultation which found that 81 per cent of people “agreed with the intention for separate single-sex toilet facilities.”

Now it appears that last week’s Supreme Court judgment might lead to the return of gender neutral loos – if only as an additional, “third” space, and quite possibly at considerable expense to the companies responsible for each building. Last week, it emerged that one council had spent £13,400 making one public lavatory block gender neutral, in 2021.

Public lavatories have been available in Britain since around the mid-19th century but initially only for men. Victorian women had to campaign to be unshackled from the “urinary leash” which meant they could only go so far before needing to return home to relieve themselves.

Female-only toilets started to emerge in the first half of the 20th century, with Selfridges being the first department store to offer public toilets for women when it opened in 1909.

But unisex toilets are a relatively recent invention, with nightclubs in the late 1990s being the first to experiment.

By the early 2000s, schools were beginning to introduce these unisex bathrooms. One of the first was Bramhall High School in Stockport, near Manchester, in 2000.

John Peckham, the head teacher at the time, suggested that the unisex cubicles opening into a shared washbasin area would prevent bullying, vandalism and smoking. But even then, parents expressed concerns that their child might be embarrassed using them or it would encourage sexual liaisons between the pupils.

The Department of Education (DfE) was also not in favour, stating that “the time is not right for the introduction of unisex toilets in our schools”. Yet just seven years later, it issued new guidance encouraging all new schools in England to fit unisex toilets.

In January 2009, University of Staffordshire started trialling gender-neutral toilets in its nightclub. “We do have transgender students here, but the new facilities are not just for them – they are for the androgynous students as well,” said Fee Wood, the student union president at the time.

Over the next decade, more unisex toilets would be fitted into academic institutions such as Lancaster, Leeds and Sheffield Universities.

But protests continued. In 2014, parents complained after Harbour Primary and Nursery School in Newhaven, East Sussex introduced unisex lavatories at the start of the school year.

Three years later, the headmaster of the £26,000-a-year Highgate School in North London, which had installed the toilets, issued an apology to parents saying: “I’m aware this change has left a number of pupils, particularly Years 7 and 8 feeling less comfortable and happy at school.”

Tracy Shaw, of Safe Schools Alliance UK, which campaigns to uphold safeguarding in schools says that unisex toilets in schools create safeguarding risks.

“Organisations are saying they need time to reflect on the Supreme Court ruling and review their policies but in the case of schools they should not need to,” she says. “Regardless of what it said in the Equality Act, schools should have been reviewing all guidance from a safeguarding point of view and resisting changes that put children at risk.

“Girls’s toilets are for girls. Gender neutral toilets that have no gap under the door are not as safe as toilets that do not have to be completely closed off to prevent voyeurism, because the lack of a gap means that collapse, self-harm or assault goes undetected. This is a safeguarding issue.”

Maya Forstater, chief executive of the Sex Matters campaign group, says, ‘It is absolutely fine to have single-user unisex options alongside dedicated male and female toilets’ Credit: Iain Masterton/Alamy Stock Photo

The gender-neutral trend was not confined to academia. It also swept through Whitehall with the Home Office changing its ten single-sex toilets in 2018 to unisex at a cost of £40,000. Some female members of staff were so unhappy they began walking to the Ministry of Communities, Housing and Local Government to use the female toilets there.

Reportedly, a note was pinned to one of the Home Office’s new toilets which read: “Polite notice: Could men using these toilets please use them with the door shut. Women are finding the use of these toilets quite distressing.”

Venues such as the Barbican Centre and The Old Vic also followed suit. While some welcomed the change, again there was backlash.

In January 2022, a YouGov poll echoed the feelings of those who had publicly opposed the changes. It showed that 87 per cent of people wanted separate toilets for men and women with 35 per cent also supporting the idea of a unisex toilet. Only seven per cent of people wanted a unisex toilet option exclusively.

Heather Binning, director of the Women’s Rights Network, says the campaign group supports the idea of unisex facilities – but not at the expense of women and girls.

“We have fought long and hard over recent years for the rights for women and girls and a specific battle has been the right to have female-only toilets,” she says. “We are the sex that copes with menstruation and pregnancy, and various problems associated with both.

Big Brother’s India Willoughby, who was born male and underwent gender reassignment surgery in 2015, said she will continue to use toilets of preferred gender identity Credit: Dave Benett

“We use the facilities for longer and are often faced with long queues. However, just as important is the right to have our privacy and dignity respected at all times and particularly when we are in a state of partial undress.

“Single sex facilities are mandatory in workplaces and schools, and whilst we support the addition of unisex toilets, these must not replace a single-sex space as they do not provide for the specific needs of women.”

Yet until organisations are able to provide this “third space”, critics of the new ruling fear that trans people will be negatively impacted.

Meanwhile some trans individuals on social media – including Big Brother’s India Willoughby – say they will still continue to use the toilets of their preferred gender identity.

Maya Forstater, the chief executive of the Sex Matters campaign group, says that “anyone using toilets designated for the opposite sex – apart from accompanied young children – is breaking rules that exist for everyone’s safety, dignity and privacy.”

While “it’s absolutely fine to have single-user unisex options alongside dedicated male and female toilets”, she adds: “Employers and service providers should not respond to the Supreme Court by replacing women’s and men’s toilets with gender-neutral facilities. This would result in worse facilities for everyone, and in many circumstances would constitute unlawful discrimination against women.”"

Earlier today, @Meta temporarily removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's video on the NEET paper leaks in India. According to media reports, a Meta spokesperson stated that the post was taken down due to an error and it had since been restored, post-haste.

The temporary removal of PM Modi's post highlights the larger issue of wrongful content takedowns by these platforms, often without any notice to users and leaving them with no meaningful recourse. These takedowns may be carried out by automated systems that have  been deployed as part of the growing due diligence obligations under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, or by way of government-issued order which reflects as a “legal request” on the platform.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has seen multiple instances of automated monitoring systems wrongfully taking down content, with no available recourse but engaging with the platform's internal appeals mechanisms and grievance officers. While high profile instances such as this are resolved quickly, ordinary users are often left high and dry. These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless. Platforms may deploy these automated systems to deal with the huge volumes of content that they have to moderate under the existing regulatory system, especially since many of these obligations are tied to the safe harbour provisions under the IT Act that exempt platforms from being liable for the content they host. However, having humans in the loop for grievance redressal would ensure that fair outcomes are delivered to all and not only to high-profile persons.

According to media reports, the Delhi Police has also identified around 450 social media accounts that allegedly shared deepfakes and AI generated content related to the protests. The Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove this kind of content shared during the CJP protests, along with other content considered "objectionable" that relates to the Prime Minister.

Such vague orders that invoke generic grounds such as “objectionable” or “offensive” are inconsistent with the safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. In the present case, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

The opacity surrounding the reasons for these takedowns goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Instead, what we see emerging through these takedowns is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where various government and law enforcement bodies decide the limits of free speech without transparency or oversight. An illustrative example is the temporary restriction faced by the @Cockroachisback’s primary Instagram handle, which was entirely blocked  on the evening of July 22. As per media reports, the account was restored after the Union Government reversed the blocking and advised the law enforcement agency that “action should be limited to specific posts or URLs instead of the entire account.”

It is not just the Prime Minister’s  post or CJP’s account that has faced such removals recently. Under the decentralised and opaque content removal regime, dozens of Instagram posts and videos related to the protests have been taken down, either by automated systems or in response to government orders, and many users have even had their accounts restricted. For these users, without high-profile attention, regaining access to their accounts or having the content restored is a long and arduous process, with no guarantee of remedy or reprieve.

LVM (state forests) got ransomed hard in June 💀 Attackers walked in through a system that hadn’t been updated in like two years, plus other software that was mid as hell since 2019. They chilled inside for 11 days, encrypted everything, dropped ~44GB of docs, emails, source code, keys and passwords. Ransom was 0.1% of yearly revenue, over 600k euros. LVM said nah. Criminal process for “impersonating” LVM, search, device seized 🚔 He lowkey got treated like the villain for doing the actual work.
Barely two months later CSDD (the traffic/vehicle agency) got hit 📉 1.2 million people’s data from payment records going back to 2008 just yeeted out the door — personal codes, names, plates, addresses, the whole bag. CERT_LV said the attackers used an internet-facing vuln and basic stuff like MFA and real pen tests was missing. Board resigned, boss said he’s out after the investigation.
Flashback to 2018: inventor Raimonds Skuruls found a broken session timeout in CSDD’s e-services that left accounts open for hours. Reported it properly. Asked for a tiny 1k euro for the effort after they checked it. Got charged with extortion, raided, years of court 🤦‍♂️ Multiple rounds of guilty/not guilty. Security pros association said the whole thing was sus and kills any motivation to report real issues.
Same pattern twice. Ancient unpatched systems. Big leaks. Independent people who actually understand the tech try to help or just explain what happened. Police show up. No real bug bounty culture, no safe harbour, just defensive energy.
Lessons weren’t learned. Class A systems getting treated like some random mid website. Until that changes the cycle stays the same: systems rot, breaches hit, and the few people trying to fix it catch the smoke 🔥

1943 Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose's Rare Speech From Tokyo

Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose’s famous radio broadcast from Tokyo on 21 June 1943, which marked a massive turning point in India's armed struggle for independence. Following a perilous journey from Germany via a submarine, Netaji arrived in Japan to take control of the Indian National Army (INA) and broadcasted this call to action directly to the people of India.

The original audio of this rare address has been preserved and released by national archives like the Prasar Bharati Central Archives, as well as historical repositories on Internet Archive.

Netaji strongly criticised Anglo-American war propaganda. He explicitly mocked British military claims on the Indo-Burma frontier, pointing out how their forces retreated as soon as counter-offensives began.

He firmly stated that Indian citizens would never compromise with British imperialism, equating compromise to accepting permanent slavery.

He announced his presence in East Asia to organize an armed rebellion from outside Indian borders, calling upon all freedom-loving Indians to prepare for the ultimate sacrifice.

Netaji underscored that Indian liberty was closely linked with the total overthrow of Anglo-American imperialism across East.

June 19, 1943 Press Conference: Two days before his broadcast, Netaji held an official press conference in Tokyo. He explained the genuine sentiments of Indians and highlighted the civilizational bonds between India and Japan.

November 1943 Greater East Asia Conference: Netaji attended this summit alongside Japan's Prime Minister Hideki Tojo. During this historic gathering, he successfully secured the sovereignty of the Provisional Government of Azad Hind and negotiated the handover of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands back to India.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

FREE SPEECH DOESN’T NEED A GOVERNMENT PERMISSION SLIP.

The Modi Government’s growing agenda for controlling what Indians can see, read, post, critique and challenge online should concern every citizen — regardless of political affiliation.

From demanding takedowns to tightening the time available to platforms to scrutinise government notices, the direction is unmistakable: comply first, question later. India’s 2026 IT-rule changes cut the takedown window for unlawful content to just three hours, while the Government has also proposed making certain official advisories legally binding on platforms. X’s own stated policy is that requests can be challenged when they are legally defective, overly broad or appear to impermissibly burden freedom of expression. (Transparency⁠)

And that is where the real problem begins for the Modi Government.

When an independent platform refuses to become an obedient extension of the State, the State’s attempts to control the narrative become visible.

No algorithm can hide that.
No press conference can spin that.
No amount of propaganda can erase that.

If the Government’s demands are genuinely about protecting citizens and enforcing legitimate law, let them withstand public scrutiny, judicial scrutiny and independent platform scrutiny.

But if criticism, dissent, inconvenient facts and uncomfortable questions are increasingly treated as “content to be removed”, then Musk’s resistance does something far more important than defending X.

It exposes this Govt’s vile intent and its surreptitious machinery.

And once the machinery is exposed, the Modi Government stands increasingly bare before the very citizens whose freedom of expression it claims to protect.

A democracy doesn’t become stronger by silencing criticism.
It becomes stronger by surviving it.

The Black Sea’s Next Casualty May Be Bread—

The widening Black Sea campaign risks turning global food supplies into collateral damage as Russia and Ukraine strike grain terminals, ports, and commercial vessels. Together, the two countries account for roughly 27 percent of global wheat exports, making prolonged disruption particularly dangerous for import-dependent states in Africa and the Middle East. A limited maritime agreement backed by Turkey, Egypt, China, and India could protect grain flows even if broader peace remains impossible. 

Yet treating both sides as equally responsible obscures how the crisis began: Moscow blockaded Ukrainian exports and weaponized food long before Kyiv brought reciprocal pressure to Russian ports. Any new corridor must therefore include credible monitoring and consequences for violations.

Apple has reportedly sent threat notifications to users in 110 countries who may have been targeted with mercenary spyware. 

What is mercenary spyware?  

Mercenary spyware is surveillance software deployed by government or law enforcement agencies to surveil individuals such as journalists, activists, politicians, and diplomats and collect sensitive information from their devices. One of the most well-known examples is Pegasus, developed by the NSO Group.

The @DoT_India notified the Telecommunications (User Identification) Rules, 2026 (“the Rules”) on 21 August 2026. The Rules mandate that telecom operators verify the facial biometric information of every person who chooses to obtain a new SIM, replace or change their details, or even surrender their number. 

(1/n)
#privacy #surveillance #biometric

It seems that the Rules, along with the circular, aim to revive the same mandates that have been struck down as illegal and unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in the past.

(9/n)
#privacy #surveillance #biometric

Such measures present a grave threat to the fundamental right to privacy for millions of Indians, as it requires private entities to collect and process troves of biometric information based on justifications that fail to satisfy the test of proportionality and necessity.

(10/n)

https://t.co/fQcMLwYL9X, a crowdsourced platform created to anonymously document alleged demands for bribes has been temporarily taken offline, citing concerns around traffic, data security, spam, duplicate entries, and misuse.

The public disclosure of alleged demands has also raised questions about the criminal liability of complainants. Under the Prevention of Corruption Act, bribing a public servant is punishable with up to seven years’ imprisonment. Those who report the demand within seven days are exempt from punishment. However, a public disclosure on a website falls outside that protection.

Speaking to @timesofindia, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 founder @mishichoudhary highlights the importance of data minimisation, security by design, and anonymity on such platforms to protect complainants' identities.
